title: Seaver v. Ransom
summary: A niece could enforce the husband’s promise to his dying wife to provide for the niece by will, where the wife signed her own will in exchange for that promise.
notes: The notes question the proposition that only the beneficiary can enforce such a promise. They discuss a promisee’s possible specific-performance action under Restatement § 307. The case should therefore not be read as announcing that a promisee necessarily loses all enforcement rights.

sections.Parties: The plaintiff was Mrs. Beman’s niece and intended beneficiary. Judge Beman was the husband who promised his wife to provide for the niece. The defendants represented his estate after he died without performing that promise.
sections.Material Facts: Mrs. Beman was dying and had a small estate consisting mainly of a house. Her husband prepared a will that gave the niece $1,000, gave him use of the house for life, and left its remainder to a charitable society. When it was read, Mrs. Beman objected that she wanted the niece to receive the house. She feared she lacked the strength to wait for a new will. Judge Beman solemnly promised that, if she signed the existing will, he would leave the niece enough in his own will to make up the difference. She signed. When he later died, his will contained no provision for the niece. The house’s value was $6,000. The niece was in poor health and had sometimes lived with the couple.
sections.Procedural History: The niece prevailed at trial on a trust theory. The Appellate Division affirmed using third-party-beneficiary contract reasoning. In 1918 the New York Court of Appeals affirmed, while explaining why the trial court’s particular property-trust theory did not fit the assets the husband had actually received.
sections.Issue: Could the niece enforce the husband’s promise although it was made to her aunt, and did the absence of suitable trust property defeat recovery?
sections.Holding: The niece could enforce the supported promise made for her benefit. The absence of property properly impressed with the proposed trust did not defeat contractual enforcement.
sections.Reasoning:
The wife supplied consideration by executing the will on the husband’s assurance. The court distinguished a trust imposed on property acquired through a promise from a personal contractual duty to provide the benefit. The husband had received only a life interest in the house, so the specific trust explanation was inadequate. His promise nevertheless remained binding.

The court considered earlier New York beneficiary categories, including debt-discharge cases and close-family provision cases. It found no persuasive reason to protect a spouse or child while excluding a beloved niece in these circumstances. The agreement was expressly designed to provide her a benefit, and she was the person substantially injured by nonperformance. Her aunt’s representatives had little practical interest in enforcing the promised provision. That combination supported enforcement directly by the niece.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Seaver extends beneficiary protection beyond the debt-discharge setting in Lawrence v. Fox. It distinguishes a gift intended for the beneficiary from an unsupported gift promise between the actual contracting parties.

topics.third-party-beneficiaries: Protects the person for whose benefit the husband made a supported promise.
topics.consideration: The aunt’s execution of her will supplies consideration even though the niece provides none.
topics.assent: An express bargain can create rights in an absent intended recipient.

mnemonic.rationale: A house promised to a niece
